87.t: Jam sessions as the training ground
87.s: Constant after-hours playing taught them, in basements and anywhere, and new arrivals were challenged.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: You know, we used to blow all night, and one of the things that I think helped most of us were we were constantly playing. We didn't make anything but we'd go out after work and play all night. The only time we weren't playing was probably when we were asleep.

87.t: Minton's, Monroe's and carrying your own rhythm section
87.s: Minton's and Monroe's held sessions, and horn players brought their own rhythm sections, but real jams meant playing with strangers.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: Up at Minton's -- used to go at Minton's. Same thing. But even before modern jazz got up at Minton's, they used to run the sessions up there. A lot of guys used to go. I used to go up there and play a lot. But all over. They had these things on 52nd Street, all around. But way before 52nd Street…

418.t: Sitting in at sessions and how it has become harder
418.s: Sitting in has gone on since the music began; now players ask whether you can play, and standards rose after the early Thirties.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: Yes. If guys were with a band that ...(?)..., they'd sit in -- to keep their chops up, you know. But now, when you go to sit in, the guys want to know "Can you play?" You have to be sure you can play something.

418.s: Sessions let players learn what others were doing and trade ideas, like a seminar, and are now rare.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: Well, they give you a chance to learn what the other guy is doing. You've got to use a little of what he's got with your stuff, and you maybe can come up with something that's another monster. Or angel. Either way you want to look at it.

412.t: Jimmy Ryan's jam sessions and Eddie Condon at work
412.s: Hodes says being heard by one's peers was important. He describes Condon's behind-the-scenes work with the press, Ernie Anderson and Milt Gabler, and standing in line to sit in.
412.ch: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (corrected typing)
412.q: Man, I got some of the darndest people -- you know, one at a time, one today, one next year, who'd insist on making good on their promises. But those were the early years. By now I'm getting acquainted with Eddie Condon, Muggsy Spanier is in town and I've sat in at Nick's, and all this bumping…

412.t: Jimmy Ryan's jam sessions and Eddie Condon at work
412.s: Hodes says being heard by one's peers was important. He describes Condon's behind-the-scenes work with the press, Ernie Anderson and Milt Gabler, and standing in line to sit in.
412.ch: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (retyped)
412.q: Man, I got some of the darndest people -- you know, one at a time, one today, one next year, who'd insist on making good on their promises. But those were the early years. By now I'm getting acquainted with Eddie Condon, is in town and I've sat in at Nick's, and all this bumping heads and breaking…

432.t: Jam sessions at the union hall and sitting in with bands
432.s: One long block about travelling, the union hall as a conservatory, and sessions.
432.q: Liotta Lyon was down there, or recorded with Al Hood when he was on this, what you call him here, Liotta Lyon. He, when you were going all over like I was, it was nice to meet everybody. You see, those bands like Jimmy Noon and all of them, they were coming down in northern part of Louisiana before…

728.s: Blue says there are fewer places to jam, but musicians should still go out and sit in.
728.q: Excuse me. There aren’t as many opportunities for musicians to go out to jam. There used to be a lot more. There’s still some, but you’ve got to get out and play with cats. You know. Even now, you go places, you go play man and it’s important. I’ll finish a gig and then find out where cats are…

605.t: Jam sessions and shedding before you play
605.s: Jam sessions were respectful and competitive; you came prepared with something to say.
605.q: I think that’s something that students really need to create for themselves, but I think one of the things, people talk about jam sessions, I think one of the things that students today don’t realize is that in the old days when we had those sessions, even though it was mostly a cooperative…

511.s: Jam sessions remain conservative and standards-based; young groups play originals.
511.q: No but that’s the other part of it. The older I get, the harder it is for me to leave the house. If I’m home I’d rather just stay home and practice or compose, so I’m not out as much. But if I’m already out and it’s close to the time when the sessions are going to start, the jam sessions are still…

460.t: Taking Julius Baker to Birdland to hear Freddie Hubbard
460.s: Laws brings Baker to Birdland to hear the Jazz Messengers and Freddie Hubbard, giving Baker new respect for jazz.
460.q: He wasn’t interested. It was I that wanted to expose him to something that’s special. Like I said, I considered him the most – the greatest virtuoso on that instrument, and I knew that he could appreciate that aspect to playing music. I knew Freddie Hubbard would display that. So I invited him one…

219.t: Jam sessions today: young players do not know how
219.s: Wein says a jam session is a performance with tradition, citing the Jazz Gallery midnight session and Delfeayo's standing big band.
219.q: A jam session is a performance. I just did something with the Jazz Gallery where I said, "You know, you people don't have to … you can do jam sessions, you got so many musicians." Made arrangements to use Michael Dorf's Jazz … the Jazz Winery and do a midnight jam session. And I went down there ……

92.t: Why the all-night sessions with Farlow, Raney and Salvador were productive
92.s: Playing among themselves allowed repeats and the exchange of ideas without audience pressure.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Oh, naturally, because we could do it over, you know. And we exchanged ideas, and it was just the-- you know, it wasn't a frantic thing where we just played. We played until we, you know, got tired and we'd stop, we'd talk, have coffee, or something, just play. It was just good fellowship, you…

93.t: J. D. the amateur-contest winner who emceed at the 81 Theater
93.s: J. D. won first prize repeatedly at the 81 Theater and once emceed for a week, which is how Ella B. Moore found him.
93.ch: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
93.q: you were great friends, you know. And it was like telling a story really, but it was on a -- it was in activities, you see. And as I say, Slim was a great tap dancer. He was a natural, see, because he taught himself all these tap dances that he knew, and he used to win the first prizes all the time.

428.t: Harlem jam sessions and the spirit of the session
428.s: He recalls daily sessions at his house with Barefield, Frankie Newton and others, and why jamming happened.
428.q: Eddie Barefield, yeah, Eddie and I've been associated for I don't know how long. We used to live near one another, and he'd have to pass where I was staying in order to get to the subway or whatever. And Tom Waley lived across the street, who was Duke's copyist, and Eddie Heywood lived in that…

78.t: How the Hawkins jam sessions worked: standards and stock arrangements
78.s: Players call standards like Basin Street and Stardust; Horace takes four-bar intros, tunes run 20 minutes, then the group discusses what happened. They did it to learn each other's styles.
78.ch: Learning from Fletcher's circle in New York
78.q: This was back then -- when the stocks -- well they were just coming out. I got all those things downstairs now, you know. Like 'Limehouse Blues,' during that era and all those things. So these guys would call out these things -- 'Basin Street,' 'Stardust,' and all these things, you know. And I…

112.t: Jam sessions at the Nest with Bechet, Dunn and Bussey
112.s: Albertson asks about sitting in; Wooding recalls musicians coming up after two in the morning to take choruses on four-beat numbers.
112.ch: South America and back in New York
112.q: No, that's what you miss. You miss that experience. Now when we were in the Nest, way back in the days of the Nest, Henry Bussey, Frank Forani, Johnny Dunn, Tommy Morris, these are fellows all used to come up. Bechet, Sidney Bechet, all of them used to come up and sit with band and play a time.…
